choices.text: Run one kitchen yourself

mem.note: ran a wedding kitchen for me

effects.log: You cook {npc}'s menu for sixty strangers. The duck is a little dry. Nobody notices, because the bride and groom fall in the pond.

choices.text: Persuade one family to move the date

effects.log: The family moves the wedding a day, for a lucky reason you invent. {npc} cooks both, and both are perfect.

events.text: {npc} is cooking one last wedding banquet before retiring, and it is for {npc}'s own grandchild. {He} wants you in the kitchen, as at the first one.

choices.text: Chop the spring onions, as before

effects.log: Two hundred spring onions. You and {npc} work side by side without needing to speak. It is the best banquet {npc} ever cooked.

choices.text: Make {npc} sit at the banquet as a guest, and cook it yourself

mem.note: made me a guest at my own banquet

effects.log: {npc} protests, then sits, then sends back the duck twice. It is a wonderful day.

events.text: {npc} has started a scarecrow contest in the fields outside town, and has entered a scarecrow dressed as the magistrate. {He} wants you to enter too, so that {he} has someone to beat.

choices.text: Build a scarecrow of {npc}

effects.log: Your scarecrow has {npc}'s hat and {npc}'s walk, somehow. The crows are terrified. {npc} is outraged and gives you the prize.

choices.text: Build a scarecrow of a tiger

effects.log: Painted stripes and a straw tail. The crows ignore it. The children of the town love it, and it wins their vote.

events.text: The scarecrow contest has grown. Farmers come from three villages. The magistrate, hearing of {npc}'s entry, has come to see it, and {npc} is hiding behind you.

choices.text: Tell the magistrate it is a tribute

effects.log: The magistrate studies the scarecrow, straightens its hat, and says it is a fair likeness. {npc} breathes again.

choices.text: Get the magistrate to judge the contest

effects.log: The magistrate, flattered, judges, and awards first prize to the scarecrow of the magistrate.

events.text: {npc} is old and the scarecrow contest is a fixture of the year now. This year the farmers have built a scarecrow of {npc}, and a scarecrow of you, standing side by side in the barley.

choices.text: Stand between them for a moment

mem.note: stood in the barley with our scarecrows

effects.log: You stand in the barley between yourself and {npc}. A crow lands on the scarecrow of you, which is a great honour.

choices.text: Bring {npc} to see

mem.note: brought me to see the scarecrows

effects.log: {npc} looks at the two scarecrows for a long time. 'Mine is better-looking,' {he} says, and is right.

events.arc: The Cat on the Temple Roof
events.text: {npc}'s cat is stuck on the temple roof and has been crying for a day. The monks will not let anyone climb the roof. {npc} is beside the gate, nearly crying too.

choices.text: Climb the roof at night

ok.log: You go up over the tiles in the dark, the cat comes to you at once, and you are both down before the monks wake. {npc} hugs the cat and you together.

mem.note: fell in the barrel for my cat

fail.log: You get the cat, slip, and slide down the tiles into a rain barrel. The monks come out. The abbot laughs until the bell is rung by accident.

choices.text: Ask the abbot with a bowl of fish

mem.note: talked to the abbot for my cat

effects.log: You sit with the abbot and talk until the abbot agrees to put a plank up for the cat. The cat comes down the plank as if it was its idea.

events.arc: The Cat on the Temple Roof
events.text: The cat is on the temple roof again. And again. It turns out the cat likes the view, and the monks have started feeding it.

choices.text: Let the cat be a temple cat

mem.note: let my cat go to the temple

effects.log: {npc} agrees, sadly, to share the cat with the temple. The cat visits {npc} every evening and goes back to the roof every morning.

choices.text: Build the cat a roof of its own on {npc}'s shed

effects.log: A little tiled roof with a view of the street. The cat moves in and stops going to the temple, mostly.

events.arc: The Cat on the Temple Roof
events.text: The cat is very old and lives on the temple roof now for good, and {npc} visits it there, by a ladder the monks keep just for {him}.

choices.text: Climb up with {npc}

mem.note: sat on the temple roof with me

effects.log: You sit on the temple roof with {npc} and an old cat. The view is very good. You understand the cat completely.

choices.text: Hold the ladder

effects.log: You hold the ladder. {npc} sits up there with the cat for an hour, talking to it, and comes down looking ten years younger.

events.text: {npc} carries sacks at the river docks and cannot read the tally boards, and the foreman cheats the porters every week. {He} asks if you would teach a few of them to read numbers, at night.

choices.text: Teach the numbers by lamplight

effects.log: Six porters, a slate and a lot of laughing. In a month they can read the tally board. The foreman is very surprised.

choices.text: Read the tally board for them each week

effects.log: You go down to the docks every payday and read the board aloud. The foreman stops cheating, mostly.

events.text: The night class has grown to twenty porters, three washerwomen and a very old boatman, and they want to learn characters now, not just numbers.

choices.text: Teach them characters

effects.log: Rice, river, silver, cheat. The boatman learns the fastest. {npc} writes a letter home for the first time.

choices.text: Find a proper teacher for them (6 taels)

effects.log: A retired clerk takes the class for a small fee, which you pay. {npc} says you should still come and listen, and you do.

events.text: {npc} is the foreman of the docks now. The tally board is written in big honest characters, and under it, every evening, {npc} teaches the new porters to read it.

choices.text: Sit in the back of the class

effects.log: {npc} teaches it exactly as you did, with the same bad jokes. You laugh at every one.

choices.text: Bring a box of slates (3 taels)

effects.log: Twenty new slates. {npc} hands them out like treasure.

events.text: {npc} has been telling people you cheat at weights in the market. It is not true. Half the street has heard it. {npc}, it turns out, believes it.

choices.text: Confront {npc} with your scales

mem.note: proved me wrong in the street

effects.log: You bring your scales and weigh a sack in front of {npc} and the whole street. Exact. {npc} goes very red.

choices.text: Let it pass and keep weighing honestly

effects.log: Months of honest weighing. The rumour fades on its own. {npc} watches you, puzzled.

events.text: {npc} has found out who really started the story: a rival trader, who used {npc} to spread it. {He} is at your door, unable to look up.

choices.text: Accept the apology

effects.log: {npc} apologises badly and sincerely. You make tea. By the end of the pot, {npc} is telling the street you are the most honest weigher in town.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to tell the street the truth

effects.log: {npc} goes door to door. It takes a week. It is the most honest week of {his} life, {he} says.

events.text: {npc} has become your fiercest defender. When anyone in the market so much as looks at your scales, {npc} appears beside them and tells the story of the rumour, at length.

choices.text: Thank {npc}, and ask {him} to stop

mem.note: asked me to stop defending them

effects.log: {npc} promises. {He} stops for a week. Then a stranger looks at your scales and the story starts again.

choices.text: Let {npc} tell it

mem.note: let me tell the rumour story

effects.log: You let {npc} tell it every time. It gets better every telling. You come out of it very well.

events.text: A troupe of travelling acrobats is camped by the road, practising: a tower of people, plates spinning on poles, a child on a rope. Their leader, {npc}, sees you watching and tosses you a plate.

choices.text: Spin the plate

ok.log: It spins. It keeps spinning. The troupe cheers. {npc} tosses you a second.

fail.log: It breaks. {npc} laughs and tosses you a wooden one, kept for beginners.

choices.text: Help them pitch the tent in the wind

effects.log: The wind is strong and the tent is huge. You hang on a rope for an hour. {npc} gives you a seat at the front of the night's show.

events.text: The acrobat troupe is performing in your town, and {npc} has a gap in the act: the person who stands at the bottom of the human tower has a bad back.

choices.text: Be the bottom of the tower

ok.log: Four acrobats on your shoulders and a child at the top waving a flag. You do not fall. The town roars.

fail.log: The tower wobbles and comes down gracefully, as they are trained to. The crowd thinks it was the act.

choices.text: Look after the bad back instead

effects.log: You know a bonesetter. The bottom of the tower is back in a week, and the troupe stays a month in your town because of it.

events.text: The troupe comes through with new faces and old ones. {npc} is grey, and does not climb any more, but the child who waved the flag is the troupe's leader now, and wants you at the front.

choices.text: Sit at the front with {npc}

effects.log: You watch the tower go up, higher than ever. {npc} names every acrobat in it and what they were like as children.

choices.text: Spin one plate, for old times

mem.note: spun a plate for me again

effects.log: You spin it. It spins. {npc} laughs and says you are hired, forty years late.

events.text: In a roadside inn the wall by the door is covered in notes left by travellers for other travellers: warnings, jokes, a poem. One note asks if anyone has seen a lost grey donkey. It is signed {npc}.

choices.text: Write an answer on the wall

effects.log: You write that you saw a grey donkey by the river ford, eating a hat. Months later, on the same wall, an answer: found it, thank you, it was my hat.

choices.text: Leave a note of your own

mem.note: left a joke on the wall

effects.log: You leave a joke. Next time you pass, someone has written underneath: terrible. Signed {npc}.

events.text: The inn wall again, and a note for you, by name, from {npc}: a whole page about the road since, the donkey, the hat, and a question about the river ford.

choices.text: Write back, a whole page

mem.note: wrote back on the inn wall

effects.log: Your two pages hang side by side. The innkeeper has started reading them to other guests. You have readers.

choices.text: Leave a gift with the innkeeper for {npc} (2 taels)

effects.log: A good straw hat, for the donkey. The innkeeper is very amused and promises to keep it safe.

events.text: Years of notes on the inn wall, and you have never met {npc}. Today at the inn there is a traveller with a grey donkey in a straw hat, reading your last note.

choices.text: Introduce yourself

effects.log: {npc} stares, then laughs, then hugs you, and the donkey eats your hat. You talk till the lamp goes out, and it is exactly like the notes.

choices.text: Leave a note instead, saying you are in the corner

effects.log: {npc} reads it, turns round slowly, and raises a cup. You raise yours. Then {npc} writes a reply anyway.

events.text: In the market a thin child, {npc}, is juggling three oranges for coppers, and dropping one every time. Nobody is paying. The child keeps trying.

choices.text: Pay a copper and give some advice

effects.log: You tell {npc} to throw lower. {npc} throws lower. Three oranges, round and round. A small crowd gathers.

choices.text: Buy {npc} a meal (1 tael)

effects.log: {npc} eats with the oranges in {his} lap, guarding them, and then juggles four for you, out of gratitude, and drops two.

events.text: {npc} has improved, and juggles five oranges in the market now, and a knife, and a teacup. The crowd is big. A troupe's manager has offered {npc} a place, and {npc} wants your opinion.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to go

effects.log: {npc} goes with the troupe. A letter comes months later, with a drawing of seven oranges in the air.

choices.text: Go and look at the troupe first

effects.log: You check the troupe: honest people, good food, a kind old clown. {npc} goes with your blessing.

events.text: A famous troupe comes to town, and its star is a juggler of nine oranges, and the star is {npc}, grown. In the middle of the act, {npc} looks out at the crowd, finds you, and throws you an orange.

choices.text: Catch it

effects.log: You catch it. The crowd roars. After the show {npc} says you were the first person who ever caught one of {his} oranges.

choices.text: Throw it back, low

effects.log: {npc} catches it and works it into the act without a drop. Ten oranges. {npc} is laughing.

events.text: On the river you meet a family who live on a boat: {npc}, the parent, and three children who swim like otters. Their boat's mooring has been taken by a merchant's barge, and they are drifting.

choices.text: Help them find a new mooring

effects.log: You walk the bank with {npc} until you find a quiet backwater with a willow. The children are in the water before the rope is tied.

choices.text: Argue with the merchant's bargemen

mem.note: stood up to the barge for us

effects.log: The bargemen laugh, then stop laughing when half the river's boat people come to listen. The barge moves.

events.text: The spring flood. You find {npc}'s boat at the willow mooring, straining at the rope, with the children tied to the mast for safety and {npc} bailing.

choices.text: Get a second line to the willow

ok.log: You wade in up to your chest and tie a second line. The boat holds. In the morning the children are swimming in the flood, which nobody can stop them doing.

fail.log: The line burns your hands but holds, just. You sit on the bank all night holding it with {npc}.

choices.text: Take the children ashore for the night

effects.log: Three wet children in your kitchen eating everything. {npc} stays with the boat. It holds.

events.text: {npc}'s children are grown, and have three boats now, moored together at the willow. They have painted your name on the willow, and they wave you aboard.

choices.text: Go aboard for a meal

effects.log: River fish, rice and the loudest family you know. {npc} tells the story of the flood, much improved.

choices.text: Swim, with the children's children

effects.log: You swim like an old otter. The children's children are unimpressed. {npc} is delighted.

events.text: A dowser, {npc}, is walking a dry village with a forked hazel stick, looking for water. The villagers are laughing. The stick suddenly dips, hard, at the corner of a field.

choices.text: Help dig where it dipped

effects.log: At twelve feet, damp earth. At twenty, water. The villagers stop laughing and start carrying stones for a well. {npc} sits on the spoil heap, smug.

choices.text: Ask how the stick works

effects.log: {npc} says {he} has no idea. Neither did {his} grandmother. It just does. {He} lets you hold it. Nothing happens.

events.text: Your own town's well has gone dry in a drought, and you send for {npc}. {He} comes with the hazel stick and the same smugness.

choices.text: Walk the town with {npc}

mem.note: found the temple water with me

ok.log: The stick dips in the temple courtyard, of all places. The monks object, then dig, then are very happy. The whole town drinks from the temple well that summer.

fail.log: The stick dips in the magistrate's garden. The magistrate refuses. A year later, the magistrate digs there secretly and finds water.

choices.text: Pay {npc} to find water for the poor quarter (5 taels)

mem.note: paid for the poor quarter's water

effects.log: Water is found behind the tannery. The poor quarter has its own well for the first time.

events.text: {npc} is old, and has brought you the hazel stick. 'It may work for you,' {he} says. 'It did not work for my children.'

choices.text: Try it

ok.log: The stick dips in your own yard. You dig, and find water. {npc} is so pleased {he} cannot speak.

fail.log: Nothing. {npc} laughs and says that is a relief, because now nobody will laugh at you in dry villages.

choices.text: Hang the stick over the door

mem.note: hung my stick over the door

effects.log: It hangs over your door. Your well never goes dry. You decide not to think about it too much.
